content: The study titled Modelling HIV self-testing for oral PrEP scale-up in Kenya: The research is part of the World Health Organization's (WHO) consolidated guidelines on differentiated HIV testing services and aims to provide insights into the health and economic implications of this approach. The provision of community-based oral PrEP has the potential to significantly expand PrEP coverage. HIV self-testing, which allows individuals to test themselves for HIV, could support this expansion by making testing more accessible. However, HIVST may have lower sensitivity compared to facility-based testing, which could lead to inappropriate PrEP use among individuals with undiagnosed HIV and, consequently, the development of drug resistance. The impact of HIVST on drug resistance in the context of PrEP scale-up has not been well understood. To address this, the researchers used an agent-based network model (EMOD-HIV) to simulate the scale-up of PrEP in western Kenya under four different HIV testing scenarios: (1) provider-administered nucleic acid testing (NAT), (2) provider-administered rapid diagnostic tests detecting antibodies (Ab RDT), (3) blood-based HIV self-testing, and (4) oral fluid HIV self-testing. These scenarios were compared to a counterfactual scenario with no PrEP implementation. The study focused on individuals aged 18 to 49 years who had at least one sexual partner and tested HIV-negative, making them eligible for PrEP. The researchers assessed the cost and health impact of rapid PrEP scale-up using these different HIV testing modalities. The results showed that achieving 29% PrEP coverage could avert 54% of HIV infections and 17% of HIV-related deaths among adults aged 18 to 49 over a 20-year period. The health impacts were similar across the different HIV testing modalities used to deliver PrEP. The proportion of drug resistance was low across all scenarios, including those using HIVST, even when accounting for background resistance to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). The budget impact of implementing PrEP using HIVST and provider-administered Ab RDT was comparable, while NAT was at least 50% more expensive. In conclusion, scaling up PrEP using HIV self-testing demonstrated similar health impacts, costs, and low risks of drug resistance compared to provider-administered rapid diagnostic tests. Stakeholders are encouraged to consider leveraging HIV self-testing as a strategy to expand PrEP access, particularly among populations at high risk of HIV infection.
